name: CML external GUI framework dependency redesign
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This conversation is an early-stage planning session for Chevron, a C++ GUI application library the person is developing. The session is explicitly structured as a collection phase — the person wants to surface multiple unresolved design concerns before tackling any of them, with the goal of identifying cross-cutting patterns and making coordinated decisions rather than addressing issues in isolation. The person noted that neglecting items like the `main()` handling risks last-minute planning, which motivated pulling it onto the list proactively.

Three items were compiled during this session. First, Chevron's CMake build scripts currently force the fetch of whichever GUI framework the user selects, regardless of whether they have a local install, a preferred version, or a patched fork — a design the person recognizes as naive and philosophically inconsistent with Chevron's own principles. Second, the handling of the application entry point (`main()`) was added to the list; the person has prior informal thoughts on an approach but no deep planning yet. Third, the question of whether Chevron should support both static and shared library builds, or commit to one, was raised — the person acknowledged limited experience with the implications and wants informed guidance before deciding. Claude framed items one and two as the same diagnostic class (Chevron imposing decisions that belong to the consumer), while distinguishing item three as a different shape: not about removing an imposition but about whether to take on ongoing internal code-side discipline in exchange for consumer flexibility. Specific concerns raised around the static/shared question included symbol visibility and export annotations, ABI stability constraints on virtual interfaces like `GUIEngine`, LTO and inlining tradeoffs, and the risk of multiple `AppProcess` instances violating process-level state invariants in certain linking scenarios.

The person prefers to collect and compile concerns before problem-solving, values when Claude reflects thinking back from a different angle even without resolving it, and explicitly welcomed that approach during this session. Communication is direct and technically substantive, using domain-specific terminology including CMake, LTO, ABI, ODR, vtable layout, `AppProcess`, `GUIEngine`, and the library name Chevron throughout.

chat_messages.text: There are some important matters that I have not addressed yet but need to come to a decision soon. I thought I'd drop some of those here so that we can hash it out. First thing I can recall, in my CML setup I may have made a really bad decision in regards to how I setup the external GUI framework dependency. A long time ago when this project was still being conceptualized (before I even came to you for the first time and made you aware of the projects existence) all I did was work on the build scripts because that was something that was going to need much care in a project anticipating a large footprint. I feel like in retrospect, I made some really naive decisions and it might need to be overhauled with a better approach. Basically, Chevron is the one that fetches the chosen GUI framework no matter what, it is forced on users of the library. The plan at the time was, "you activate the appropriate CMake option during configure and my build setup would take it from there." But I have come to realize that isn't smart because then if someone already has a local installation of the source for use, they are forced to have it fetched from GitHub anyway (a really big repository potentially; that's my experience with wxWidgets). Additionally, what if they want to use a different version than what I specify in the build scripts? Everything about the initial approach I took is not sitting well with me, it did not age well at all and now I think it is an important thing that needs to be fixed soon. I guess this turned into a rant so I only managed to get one of these important matters out for now, I'll let you read this first and come back with more. But at least you now have an idea of the kinds of things (not necessarily just CMake but general library-wide matters) that I want to drop here. I say drop because I know this is not the end of the things and so I want to get most of them out to you first to compile a small list before actually tackling them. Perhaps there are cross-cutting concerns or something and we can play our hand right and make some really great moves from this to continue Chevron in the direction that it is starting to head in. This library has a very specific ideology and philosophy of its development (how things should be done) and it takes pride in the benefits that come from it. There is more but this has gotten rather long, and the next one likely is too.

chat_messages.text:
Jamon's pointing out that Chevron's current approach to handling GUI framework dependencies is flawed—it aggressively fetches frameworks like wxWidgets during configuration, which forces users to re-download large repositories even if they already have local installations, and prevents them from using alternative versions. He's recognizing this feels overly prescriptive and needs rethinking.

He's also signaling this is just one of several library-wide design issues he wants to surface before diving into solutions, so he's asking me to acknowledge the concern and stay ready for the next topic rather than jump into CMake strategy proposals right now. The core issue is the same philosophical violation as Chevron taking over main() — the library is imposing a decision that should belong to the user. Whether someone's using a custom wxWidgets build, a system package, a monorepo vendored copy, or a patched fork, they all hit the same wall, and none of those are unreasonable scenarios. This directly contradicts Chevron's own principle of giving users control, not taking it away.

I notice this and the main() decision share an underlying pattern — the user owns their environment, and Chevron provides infrastructure within it. Jamon's in collection mode right now, gathering items before diving into solutions, and he's explicitly said walking through his thinking helps him organize it. So I should engage with what he's laying out rather than jump straight to proposing fixes. He's got three main things on his mind: how to handle external GUI framework dependencies in CMake without forcing a fetch, what design approach makes sense for main(), and whether to support both static and shared library builds and what that means for the codebase.

On the static versus shared question, he's asking the real underlying questions — what does it actually mean to give users both options, what code-level concerns come up, and whether he should just pick one? He's being honest that he doesn't have enough experience to decide this alone, and he's looking for engagement, not just acknowledgment. He likes when I reflect his thinking back from a different angle. So I should add main() to the list, then dig into what's actually at stake with the static versus shared decision without trying to resolve it yet, and watch for any threads that connect across these three topics.

The core tension is that static linking means Chevron's code gets baked into each consumer's binary with no runtime dependency, while shared linking makes Chevron a runtime dependency that needs to be deployed alongside the consumer. But the code-side implications are where it gets thorny — symbol visibility becomes pervasive (every public API needs export macros on Windows, visibility attributes on Unix), templates and inline functions create ODR headaches across DLL boundaries, and global state like AppProcess becomes genuinely painful if Chevron is shared and multiple consumers each statically link it elsewhere.

There's also the C++ ABI minefield: passing standard library types across the boundary requires consumer and library to agree on things like runtime library flavor and debug/release matching, exceptions can propagate badly depending on platform and compiler flags, and if Chevron itself supports a plugin architecture with multiple backends, that interaction layer adds another dimension of complexity to the linking strategy.

Then there's the operational side—static initialization order gets messy with shared libraries on Windows, proper versioning and SONAME management becomes a build system concern, and shared linking eliminates opportunities for the compiler to inline and optimize across translation units, whereas static linking preserves those gains.

The real strategic question is whether to offer both static and shared options. That signals flexibility to consumers, but it demands disciplined API design from the start—careful symbol visibility, stable ABI surfaces, and a clear split between what lives in headers versus what gets compiled. Different libraries take different philosophical stances here, and that choice shapes everything downstream.

There's a subtle distinction emerging: the first two concerns were about not imposing constraints that rightfully belong to the user, but the static-versus-shared question is different—it's about whether to *offer* flexibility that carries genuine internal costs for the library author. The principle of user freedom is the same, but the cost structure isn't. main() is well-placed on the list — easier to pin down once when you focus on it than to keep half-thinking about it under time pressure.

On static vs shared: the deployment-level choice is straightforward — static bakes Chevron's object code into the consumer's binary, shared makes it a runtime dependency. But underneath that sits a harder question about what it means for the library's source code to actually support both modes, because the costs don't map cleanly onto the user-choice items already listed.

The CMake fetch issue and main() are both fundamentally about not deciding things that aren't yours to decide, but the static/shared question cuts deeper — it's not just a matter of letting users choose, it imposes real structural costs on the library itself.

Committing to both means designing with both in mind forever. That commitment has concrete code weight: symbol visibility needs explicit export/import annotations on Windows especially, and anything crossing the library boundary in a shared build — return types, parameter types, exception types — requires careful ABI discipline that you can completely sidestep if you commit to static-only.

Static linking also unlocks cross-boundary inlining and LTO that shared linking can't achieve, which matters significantly for Chevron's performance-sensitive memory subsystem. And since Chevron is already a multi-backend library, if both Chevron and backend implementations are independently built shared libraries, the virtual interface between them crosses two ABI boundaries, making vtable layout a load-bearing detail.

On MSVC, mismatches in runtime library selection between Chevron and consumers cause subtle failures in shared builds, requiring either documentation or configure-time enforcement. The trickiest issue is process-level state — Chevron's AppProcess is designed to be one-per-process, but if two independently-built consumers statically link Chevron into their own dynamic libraries and both end up in the same process, each gets its own AppProcess, violating the library's invariant. The nature of this problem shifts depending on how Chevron is built and consumed.

The real question is what kind of consumer I'm designing Chevron for — an SDK shipped to many third-party applications leans toward shared libraries, a vendored single executable leans static, and trying to support both requires upfront discipline. Rather than deciding aesthetically, I should frame it as: what's my primary consumer, and how much code-side discipline am I willing to invest to keep both options viable?

On static vs shared — walking through it as you invited. At the deployment level the choice is simple: static gives the consumer a binary with Chevron's object code baked in, shared makes Chevron a runtime dependency the consumer must keep around. The interesting question is what it actually means *for the library's source code* to commit to supporting both, because the cost structure is different from the user-choice items already on the list.

The CMake fetch issue and the `main()` decision are both fundamentally "stop deciding things that aren't yours to decide." Once Chevron stops deciding, the cost to Chevron is essentially zero — you just don't do the thing. Static-or-shared is a different shape entirely: offering both is a *commitment by Chevron* to design with both in mind, forever. That commitment has ongoing weight on the source.

The most concrete piece is symbol visibility. On Windows especially, every public symbol that crosses the library boundary needs explicit export/import annotation, typically behind a single `CHEVRON_API` macro that expands differently depending on whether you're building the library, consuming it shared, or consuming it static. Skip this and the shared build won't link. Commit to static-only and the entire concern evaporates.

Beneath that lives an ABI discipline cost. Anything that crosses from Chevron into user code in a shared build — types, layouts, virtual interfaces — becomes part of an implicit ABI commitment. Adding a virtual method to `GUIEngine` is a binary-breaking change in a shared world. In a static-only world it's a recompile. This bears directly on Chevron because the `GUIEngine` virtual interface and the plugin-shaped backend topology are both load-bearing parts of the design. If Chevron and a backend implementation are each independently built as shared libraries, the vtable layout of `GUIEngine` becomes a load-bearing detail across two ABI seams.

Two more worth flagging. Performance: static linking opens cross-boundary inlining and LTO that shared linking cannot, which matters more here than in a typical library given how performance-sensitive the memory subsystem is. And state-across-the-boundary: Chevron has process-level state by design — `AppProcess` is one-per-process. If Chevron is built shared and loaded once, that invariant holds naturally. If two consumers each statically link Chevron into their own DLLs and meet inside a single process (plugin hosts, embedded scenarios), each ends up with its own `AppProcess`, violating an invariant the library claims to enforce. The shape of that problem changes with how Chevron is built and consumed.

So the question "should this library have stuck to one or the other" is fair, and there's no universal answer — it depends on who Chevron is for. A library shipped as part of an SDK consumed by many third-party applications tends to lean shared (Qt is the obvious example). A library vendored into a single executable tends to lean static. A library that wants to keep the door open pays the discipline tax up front, in code, forever.

When you come back to this one, the framing I'd suggest is: *what kind of consumer am I designing Chevron for, and how much ongoing code-side discipline am I willing to pay to leave that choice open?* That makes the answer falsifiable rather than aesthetic. Onto the list it goes — ready for the next.

Beneath that lives an ABI discipline cost. Anything that crosses from Chevron into user code in a shared build — types, layouts, virtual interfaces — becomes part of an implicit ABI commitment. Adding a virtual method to `GUIEngine` is a binary-breaking change in a shared world. In a static-only world it's a recompile. This bears directly on Chevron because the `GUIEngine` virtual interface and the plugin-shaped backend topology are both load-bearing parts of the design. If Chevron and a backend implementation are each independently built as shared libraries, the vtable layout of `GUIEngine` becomes a load-bearing detail across two ABI seams.

Two more worth flagging. Performance: static linking opens cross-boundary inlining and LTO that shared linking cannot, which matters more here than in a typical library given how performance-sensitive the memory subsystem is. And state-across-the-boundary: Chevron has process-level state by design — `AppProcess` is one-per-process. If Chevron is built shared and loaded once, that invariant holds naturally. If two consumers each statically link Chevron into their own DLLs and meet inside a single process (plugin hosts, embedded scenarios), each ends up with its own `AppProcess`, violating an invariant the library claims to enforce. The shape of that problem changes with how Chevron is built and consumed.

So the question "should this library have stuck to one or the other" is fair, and there's no universal answer — it depends on who Chevron is for. A library shipped as part of an SDK consumed by many third-party applications tends to lean shared (Qt is the obvious example). A library vendored into a single executable tends to lean static. A library that wants to keep the door open pays the discipline tax up front, in code, forever.

When you come back to this one, the framing I'd suggest is: *what kind of consumer am I designing Chevron for, and how much ongoing code-side discipline am I willing to pay to leave that choice open?* That makes the answer falsifiable rather than aesthetic. Onto the list it goes — ready for the next.
